opus-5.5.text:
So for me, compositionality is really the central mechanism that lets a learner get more out of its experience than it put in. The basic intuition is that if you've learned a set of reusable pieces, whether those are concepts, functions, skills, or subroutines, and you've also learned how those pieces fit together, then a genuinely new situation often isn't new all the way down. It's a new arrangement of things you already understand. And the space of arrangements grows combinatorially, so a modest library of well-chosen parts can cover an enormous range of situations you've never directly seen.

That's a big part of why I've gravitated toward program synthesis and program induction as a framework. Programs are compositional by construction. You've got primitives, you've got ways of combining them, and the meaning of the whole is determined by the meaning of the parts and how they're put together. So if you frame learning as inferring a program that explains your data, you get a kind of generalization for free that's hard to get from purely interpolative models. A system that's learned what "repeat" means and what "draw a line" means can draw a spiral it's never seen, as long as it can figure out the right composition.

But I think the more interesting part, and what we tried to get at with work like DreamCoder, is that compositionality alone isn't sufficient. You also need to learn the right building blocks. If your primitives are too low-level, then the programs you need for realistic problems are astronomically long and search becomes hopeless. So there's a kind of bootstrapping dynamic: you solve some problems, you look across those solutions for recurring structure, you abstract that structure into new reusable components, and now problems that were previously out of reach become short programs in your enriched language. The library grows, and with it the set of things you can generalize to. In a sense the system is learning its own representational vocabulary, and that vocabulary is what determines what counts as "near" versus "far" in terms of generalization.

The other piece is that you need some learned intuition for how to compose things, because even with good abstractions, the combinatorial space is still huge. That's where neural networks come in really naturally, not as the thing that does the generalizing directly, but as a guide that learns which compositions are likely to be useful given the problem in front of you. So I tend to think of it as a partnership: symbolic, compositional structure gives you systematic, out-of-distribution generalization, and learned neural intuition makes searching that structure tractable.

And I'd say this also connects to how humans seem to handle novelty. When people face a new problem, they don't usually start from scratch, and they also don't just pattern-match to the nearest thing they've seen. They recombine. They take a strategy from one domain and a concept from another and put them together in a way that fits the new situation. To me, building machines that can do that kind of flexible recombination, and that can grow their own repertoire of components over time, is one of the most promising routes toward systems that can actually handle situations that look nothing like their training data.

r001.rationale: The response says a learner can combine previously learned reusable pieces in new arrangements to handle situations it has never directly seen.

r002.rationale: It discusses novelty and out-of-distribution situations, but does not identify changing environments that reuse underlying causal mechanisms as a setting where compositional knowledge is especially important.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about compositionality is that it's basically the thing that lets you get out of distribution for free, or at least cheaply. If you've learned a set of pieces, and you've learned how those pieces combine, then the space of things you can represent is exponentially larger than the set of things you've actually seen. That's the whole promise. You see a finite number of situations during training, but the number of situations you can handle is combinatorial in the number of primitives you've acquired.

And I think the key word there is "represent." A lot of the discussion around compositionality gets framed as a property of the model, like, is the network compositional or not. But I find it more productive to think of it as a property of the representation, or the language, that the learner is working in. If you're learning programs, compositionality is just built in, because programs are made of subroutines and you can recombine them. The hard part isn't getting compositionality, it's learning the right primitives, learning the right library, so that the novel situations you actually encounter are short to express in terms of what you already have.

That's really the thing I keep coming back to. There's this interplay between the library you've built up and what counts as a new situation. If I have the right abstractions, then something that looks totally novel from the outside is actually just a small recombination of stuff I already know. If I have the wrong abstractions, the same situation might require a huge, improbable search. So learning to handle new situations is, in a sense, learning to make new situations not new. You're growing a vocabulary that compresses your experience and, hopefully, compresses the future too.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that compositionality works best when it's paired with search. Having the pieces isn't enough. You need some process, whether that's enumerative search, or a neural network guiding the search, or in the limit just a big model doing something like in-context reasoning, that actually finds the composition that fits the new situation. Where I think the neural and symbolic worlds meet is right there: the neural part learns what's likely, the compositional structure gives you the ability to generalize beyond what you've seen, and the search is what bridges the two when the new case isn't just a nearest neighbor of an old one.

r001.rationale: The response says learned pieces and their combinations let a learner handle situations it has not seen, with the number of representable situations growing combinatorially.

r002.rationale: It discusses novel situations and recombining learned primitives, but does not identify changing environments that reuse underlying causal mechanisms as a setting for adaptation.

astra-6.text:
I think compositionality is one of the main ways we can explain how learning gets you beyond the situations you’ve already experienced. You learn pieces of knowledge that can be reused, and then a new situation calls for putting those pieces together in a different way. Programming is a particularly clear example: you can write a program you’ve never seen before using functions and operations that you already understand.

But that pushes the question back a little bit, because where do those pieces come from? We don’t necessarily want to hand the learner a fixed set of primitives and say, “Everything you’ll ever need is a combination of these.” Part of learning should be discovering useful abstractions—recognizing that a pattern you’ve constructed several times deserves to become a reusable component itself.

And then there’s the problem of finding the right composition. Having the building blocks doesn’t mean you can efficiently search through all the ways of combining them. So I see learning and compositionality as working together: a compositional representation gives you a space of possible solutions, and learning gives you the abstractions and the guidance that make that space tractable. That’s a promising route to handling new situations, although it isn’t by itself a guarantee of generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says learned pieces of knowledge can be reused and combined in new ways to handle situations beyond those already experienced, including a program never seen before.

r002.rationale: It does not identify changing environments that reuse underlying causal mechanisms as a setting for compositional knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compositionality gives you a way to handle a new situation without having to learn everything about it from scratch. You’ve learned some pieces, and you’ve learned ways of putting those pieces together. A new situation can then involve a combination you haven’t encountered before, even though the ingredients are familiar.

Programming gives us a particularly concrete example. You can understand every operation in a program and still never have seen that particular program. And by composing those operations, you can express a new behavior. The interesting learning problem is: where do those operations come from? We shouldn’t necessarily assume that the learner starts with exactly the right building blocks. Part of learning is discovering abstractions that make future problems easier to express and solve.

So I see a kind of feedback loop. You solve problems using the concepts you have, notice recurring structure in those solutions, and turn that structure into new concepts. Those concepts then let you reach problems that were previously out of reach. Compositionality is powerful because it supports that process, but it doesn’t by itself tell you which compositions are useful or how to find them. That’s where learning and search come in.

r001.rationale: It says a new situation can combine familiar learned pieces in a way the learner has not encountered before, enabling new behavior without learning everything from scratch.

r002.rationale: It does not mention changing environments or adaptation through reuse of underlying causal mechanisms.
